Border stories

Two passports, one closed return route: a driver's story from the Belarus–Poland border

A real driver's account reveals why U.S. passports, Russian citizenship, Belarusian visas and Polish border restrictions must be checked separately before departure.

ComfortLine·Legal sources checked · 03.11.2026
Important: information only — not an official source

This article is for personal information and trip planning only. ComfortLine is not a government authority, and this page is not an official legal source, legal advice or a guarantee of entry. Rules, border crossings and exceptions can change, sometimes without notice. Always consult the linked original government documents and the competent border, visa and consular authorities immediately before travelling. Admission is decided by the authorities.

The driver's story: a missing Russian passport

A ComfortLine driver reported a journey from Poland to Belarus involving passengers travelling with U.S. passports. During passport control in Belarus, officers asked about their Russian passports; the passengers said they had left those documents at home. They also had Belarusian visas. The driver feared that, without appropriate documents, they might have faced problems both entering Belarus and returning to Poland.

This is an anonymised first-hand report, not an established court or administrative finding. We have not inspected the travellers’ documents or the border decision. We cannot establish why Belarusian officials requested the Russian passports, whether the visas changed the outcome, or whether these travellers qualified for a Polish exception. The legal risk, however, deserves attention.

A U.S. passport does not automatically permit entry from Belarus into Poland

U.S. nationals normally benefit from visa-free short visits to the Schengen area. But Polish Border Guard guidance imposes a separate restriction on entry to Poland at the Belarusian border: third-country nationals generally need to fall within a permitted category under §3(2) of Poland’s border-traffic regulation. The U.S. State Department specifically warns that U.S. citizens entering Poland from Belarus must meet an exception. [1] [2]

Possible exceptions depend on individual status and evidence—for example, qualifying residence rights, family connections or other expressly recognised grounds. A U.S., Israeli or Grenadian passport is not 'banned from Poland' in general; the problem is this particular entry direction and legal basis. An ordinary Schengen visa waiver alone is not sufficient to resolve it. [1] [2]

Dual citizenship and the Belarusian entry question

A person with U.S. and Russian citizenship must establish which documents Belarus requires for entry and exit, and which documents the next destination will accept. A Belarusian visa in a U.S. passport is not a substitute for a Russian passport if authorities legally require that passport; equally, it does not grant permission to enter Poland.

The account does not establish the Belarusian legal basis for asking to see the Russian passports. Travellers should obtain individual guidance from Belarusian consular or border authorities rather than relying on assumptions about dual nationality. The U.S. Department of State currently advises Americans not to travel to Belarus (Level 4) and warns about limited consular assistance and unexpected border closures. [8] [10]

Russian non-biometric passports: Poland and Lithuania have different dates

Poland stopped recognising Russian non-biometric diplomatic and service passports on 1 January 2026, followed by ordinary non-biometric passports on 1 April 2026. Lithuania's corresponding restriction began on 1 June 2025, with a later transition for certain residence-permit holders and a specific rail-transit exception. Always verify the applicable exceptions. [3] [4]

Do not confuse two different requirements: under Article 6 of the Schengen Borders Code, a travel document for a short visit generally must have been issued within the preceding 10 years. That does not mean it must have a ten-year validity period. The separate question is whether the country recognises the particular document as biometric. [5]

Ukrainian passports: distinguish visa-free travel from other legal grounds

For ordinary visa-free short visits, Ukrainian nationals require a qualifying biometric passport. That is not the same as saying every Ukrainian citizen must always possess a biometric passport in every border situation. A visa, residence status or an applicable humanitarian mechanism may create different legal circumstances. [6] [7]

EU guidance on protection for people fleeing Ukraine concerns particular humanitarian situations and routes. Do not automatically treat it as an exemption applicable to a journey into the EU from Belarus. Check the receiving country's rules and the traveller's actual status. [7]

Lithuania is not Poland

Poland's §3(2) restriction should not be copied onto the Lithuanian border. Lithuania has its own nationality-, document- and security-based entry measures, and border-crossing points can change operational status. A U.S. or Israeli passport does not, by itself, establish either guaranteed admission or a blanket prohibition at Lithuania's border with Belarus. [4] [9]

Check each direction and each intended checkpoint separately, including whether passenger vehicles may use it. A visa or residence permit may be relevant but never eliminates the individual border assessment under the Schengen Borders Code. [5] [9]

Plan the return journey before the outward journey

Confirm every citizenship and carry the travel documents relevant to each jurisdiction. Check the validity and recognition of each passport, visas or residence permits, the legal ground for entry at the chosen Polish or Lithuanian crossing, and any sanctions or vehicle restrictions. Verify that the checkpoint is actually open for your mode of transport.

Most importantly, do not assume that because you could leave Poland and enter Belarus, you can automatically return by the same road. Seek guidance from the competent authorities before setting off, and prepare a legally viable alternative route rather than relying on an unverified assumption. [1] [2] [8]

Before leaving: a practical checklist

  • List all citizenships and carry all relevant valid travel passports.
  • Check the Belarusian entry and exit basis for each traveller.
  • Check the specific legal exception or permission for re-entry to Poland, or the applicable Lithuanian rules.
  • Verify biometric recognition, passport validity, visas and residence documents.
  • Confirm checkpoint opening and permitted transport types for both directions.
  • Review official notices again immediately before departure.
